text: One last thing before the verdict, and it is a demonstration of the single most useful habit in this whole week. Working in a loop.
Because the temptation, when something comes back nearly right, is to accept it and quietly live with the bit that annoys you. Do not. Say the annoying bit out loud, specifically, and send it back.

Notice how that feedback is phrased. Not this is bad. Not make it better. Here is the exact thing that is wrong, here is why it is wrong, and here is the standard I am holding it to. Every one of those three parts is doing work.

And that is the job, in one sentence. Not writing the thing. Describing precisely what is wrong with the thing in front of you, which is a skill you already have from every other part of your working life.
So I sent that, and it changed three files. Not a rewrite. Three small edits, in the three places that decide how wide a column is and how much space sits around it. Precise feedback, precise change.
And here is the board after. The columns fill the width now. That dead space on the right is gone, and the whole thing looks like it was meant to be that size.
Now look at the left edge. The cards in the first column are still touching the window. It did one of the two things I asked for, and told me it was done.

I want to be clear that this is not me catching it out. This is the loop working exactly as it is supposed to. It made a change, I went and looked, and looking found the half that was not finished. If I had accepted its word for it, that edge would have shipped.

And notice why I could catch it at all. I named two specific things. The padding, and the width. Which meant that when it came back I had two specific things to check, and I could see immediately that one of them had not moved.
Vague feedback gets you a vague answer that you cannot grade. Make it bad, and you have nothing to check. Two named faults, and you can count them off.
So it goes back a second time, with one line, naming the one thing left. And that is the rhythm of the whole three weeks. Not one perfect instruction. A short loop, run until it is right.
That is four builds of the same brief, and before I give you a verdict I want to give you the caveat, because the caveat is more useful than the verdict.

These four runs did not use the same model. One had a frontier tier, one had whatever the free plan handed it, and the others sat somewhere in between. So some of what you just watched is a difference between harnesses, and some of it is simply a stronger model doing a better job. Those two things look identical from the outside, and the only defence against confusing them is to say out loud which model ran.
Which is why the honest headline of today is not that one of these tools won.
So. Four builds, four harnesses, one brief. Here is the grid we have been filling in all day.

It is that they are all, structurally, the same thing. A sidebar you can drag wider. A place to type. Usually a planning step and an execution step, though not always as separate modes. And a plain text file in your repository that tells the agent how to behave, which almost all of them now agree to read.

And here is the thing I want you to take away, which is not the winner. Look at how similar the rows are. The brief is the same file in nearly every case. The prompt is identical. The checks all pass. What differs is the furniture and the permission dialogue.
Three of these four are the same editor underneath. Two of them are literally forks of it and one is an extension inside it. That is not an accident and it is not going to reverse.

Every one of them gives you a panel you can drag wider, a place to type, some notion of planning before doing, a dial for how much permission it needs, and a plain text file in your repository that tells it how to behave.

Look back at what actually changed between the four. The brief did not change. The prompt did not change. The five checks did not change. What changed was the furniture, the permissions dialogue, and the model. That is the whole difference, and it is much smaller than the marketing on any of the four websites suggests.

That last one is the important convergence, and it happened faster than anybody expected. A year ago every tool wanted its own special configuration file with its own special name. Today they have very largely agreed, and the holdout in this comparison has stopped holding out since the course I built this from was recorded.
Which means the work you did writing that brief is not an investment in one product. It is portable. Change tools next month and the file comes with you.
So, choosing. And I am going to give you the boring answer, because it is the correct one.

Choose the one your team already uses, so you can ask somebody when you get stuck. Or the one your employer already pays for, because that argument is already won. Or the one you can log into right now without reaching for a card. Any of those three is a better reason than a benchmark.

So how do you choose. Honestly, mostly on things that have nothing to do with capability. Which one your team already uses. Which one your employer already pays for. Which one you can already log into. Which keyboard you already know. Pick on that, and know that the skill you build in one of them transfers to the others in about an afternoon.

And do not agonise, because the skill transfers. Everything you learned today about writing a brief, reading a plan, watching a permission prompt and checking a claim works in all four of them, and it will work in the one that launches next month too.
And that is the real reason we did the same build four times. Not to crown a winner. To show you that the tool is the least interesting variable in the room.
Which is exactly why the course turns here. Three days in, you have seen the products, and the products turned out to be the least interesting variable in the room.

Which is where the course turns. Three days in, you have seen the products. From here on it is technique. How to write a brief that does not need a follow up. How to make an agent prove a fix instead of claiming one. How to work in a loop instead of one long hopeful prompt. Those skills do not expire when the next IDE launches, and one will launch before you finish this course.

From tomorrow it is technique. How to write a brief that does not need a follow up. How to make an agent prove a fix instead of announcing one. How to work in a loop rather than firing one long hopeful prompt and hoping. How to know when to stop.
None of those skills expire when the next editor launches. And one will launch before you finish this course, which is not a joke, it is a scheduling observation.
Tomorrow we stop comparing and start building, with one tool, on something bigger than a board with five columns. Bring the file. You are twenty percent of the way through.
